works.abstract: Microplastics undergo continued physicochemical transformation under environmental stresses such as mechanical abrasion, thermal cycling, and ultraviolet (UV) radiation. However, their degradation is commonly evaluated using population-averaged or independent endpoint measurements, which cannot directly reveal how individual particles evolve over time or how degradation trajectories differ among particles. Here, we longitudinally tracked the degradation of individual poly(ethylene terephthalate) microplastics (PET MPs) during 45 days of accelerated UV-C aging. Low-vacuum scanning electron microscopy (LV-SEM) and high-magnification digital microscopy (DM) enabled repeated morphological characterization of the same particles, while atomic force microscopy (AFM) PinPoint™ mapping provided particle-level measurements of nanoscale surface roughness and local apparent Young’s modulus. The nine tracked PET MPs exhibited markedly heterogeneous degradation trajectories: after 45 days, seven particles retained approximately 25–56% of their initial projected area, whereas two had no detectable projected area remaining. Mean fractional area loss increased across successive 15-day intervals, indicating increasing susceptibility to material loss with accumulated aging. Associations between particle morphology and subsequent material loss also varied across aging intervals, although these relationships are considered exploratory given the small particle population. AFM measurements further revealed substantial local nanomechanical heterogeneity and an overall decrease in apparent Young’s modulus from Day 0 to Day 45. These results highlight the value of longitudinal same-particle measurements for resolving both temporal evolution and particle-to-particle heterogeneity during accelerated PET microplastic degradation.
works.title: Longitudinal single-particle tracking and nanomechanical characterization of PET microplastic degradation under accelerated UV aging
